title: The Moon is drifting away from Earth by 3.8 cm a year
body: The Moon’s gravity raises tidal bulges on Earth. Because Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, those bulges get dragged slightly ahead of the Moon, and their pull tugs it forward, nudging it into a gradually higher orbit. In return, the Moon’s pull on the bulges acts like a brake on Earth’s spin. The result: the Moon slips about 3.8 cm farther away every year, while our days slowly get longer.

slides.heading: Measured with mirrors
slides.text: Apollo 11, 14 and 15 crews left reflectors on the Moon. Observatories fire lasers at them and time the roughly 2.5-second round trip with great precision.

slides.heading: Earth pays the price
slides.text: The same tidal tug slows Earth’s rotation, adding a little under 2 milliseconds to the length of a day every century.

slides.question: Why does the Moon keep climbing into a higher orbit?
options: Earth’s tidal bulges tug it forward
The Sun’s gravity drags it outward
The solar wind pushes on it
slides.explanation: Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, so the tidal bulges are dragged slightly ahead of the Moon and their pull tugs it forward. In return, Earth’s spin slows and days lengthen.

slides.heading: Which mission left no laser reflector?
slides.explanation: Apollo 11, 14 and 15 each left a reflector that observatories still bounce lasers off. Apollo 17 did not; two Soviet Lunokhod rovers carried smaller arrays.
